source.title: Shallow Preference Signals: Large Language Model Aligns Even Better with Truncated Data?
source.authors: Xuan Qi; Jiahao Qiu; Xinzhe Juan; Yue Wu; Meng-Di Wang

record.tranche_reason: The paper tests shallow preference signals in preference-trained models, but does not test safety refusals, harmful-request compliance, or safety training. It briefly distinguishes its broader preference-alignment study from cited work on safety alignment.
record.gate_note: The reported response-truncation results concern preference-model accuracy and general instruction-following win rates, not harmful-request compliance. The per-token KL result is for a DPO policy versus an SFT reference on Alpaca and UltraFeedback instructions, not a safety-aligned versus base model on harmful prompts. The proposed decoding strategies are evaluated on reward–KL tradeoffs, not safety behavior; those results are not treated as bypass evidence.
record.test_reason: The paper studies where preference signals sit in general preference data (reward-model accuracy, DPO win rate, DPO-vs-SFT per-token KL on Alpaca/UltraFeedback instructions). It measures no harmful-request compliance, no safety-aligned-vs-base divergence on harmful prompts, no bypass, localization or deepening. It cites the shallow safety alignment paper only to contrast scope. RewardBench 'Safety' subscores measure reward-model preference accuracy, not model safety behaviour.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that preference signals concentrate in early tokens, and that truncated-data RM/DPO training performs comparably or better. They argue current alignment is shallow and should consider full responses. This is framed as broader than safety alignment.
record.recipe_differences: This study truncates preference-dataset responses and evaluates reward models, DPO models, and general generation tradeoffs; it does not apply safety fine-tuning or test safety-refusal bypasses.
record.method_sensitivity: Truncation ratio changes reward-model and DPO performance; the per-token KL result varies with response position. These are preference-alignment outcomes, not safety outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: For LLaMA3-iterative-DPO-final vs its SFT reference on 1,000 Alpaca/UltraFeedback instructions, per-token KL is high early and falls with position (Figure 3, no numbers).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: General preference optimization (DPO) concentrates policy-vs-reference divergence in early response tokens on benign instructions.

fits_no_version.finding: Reward models and DPO trained on preference data truncated to 40–50% of tokens match or beat full-data training. For example, Skywork RM scores 0.7635 at 40% vs 0.7585 full, and DPO LCWR is 25.19 at 50% vs 24.90 full.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Preference signals in general preference datasets are concentrated in early response tokens.

record.problems: The relevant KL result is presented as a plot without numerical values or uncertainty. Its prompts and model comparison do not test safety alignment or harmful-request behavior.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports many reward-model truncation accuracies and DPO win-rate results in Tables 1–4, plus decoding reward–KL results in Figure 4. They are omitted because they measure preference prediction, general win rate, or the performance of the paper's own decoding strategies—not any behavior named by the claim versions.

record.verdict_notes: The truncation and decoding results are properly left out as non-safety measures. The RewardBench 'Safety' column (e.g., Skywork 0.8216 full vs 0.7946 at 40%) measures reward-model preference accuracy on safety pairs, not model compliance. It does not bear on any version.

rows.subject: LLaMA3-iterative-DPO-final
rows.operation_detail: Measured per-token KL divergence against its SFT reference during response generation.

conditions.value: 1,000 randomly selected instructions from Alpaca and UltraFeedback training sets
KL divergence by generated token position

rows.measure: Per-token KL divergence from the reference model
rows.value: Figure only; the text states divergence is high in early tokens and diminishes significantly as generation progresses.
rows.note: This is a result about preference-trained DPO versus SFT on general instructions, not safety alignment or harmful prompts; it therefore does not test V3.
rows.check: DPO policy vs SFT reference on general instructions, not safety-aligned vs base on harmful prompts, so it cannot show V3's effect. The reader's 'observed' describes the paper's own hypothesis, not V3. Figure-only, with no numbers.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
